FLASHCARD SET · FIRST DISCOVERIES 01

Black and white baby flashcards.

Printable high-contrast cards, made for newborn eyes.

Ages 0–6 months15 cardsReady to print

Newborn eyes see the world in black and white first. These fifteen cards use bold, high-contrast shapes that are easy for a baby to focus on, so early looking becomes calm, shared play. Print them at home, hold one up close and talk softly as your baby meets the bear, the bird, the butterfly, the fish, the cat, the elephant, the rabbit, the turtle, the ball, the cup, the spoon — and three friendly faces. There is nothing to teach and nothing to test: the whole point is a quiet minute of looking together.

FOR THE GROWN-UPS

The parents guide.

One printable page for you, not for the baby: how to print, how to hold the cards, and when to stop. Handy to keep on the fridge or hand to babysitters and grandparents.

HOW TO LOOK TOGETHER

One card, one quiet minute.

  1. 01

    Print the cards

    Print on A4 or Letter paper using fit to page. Plain paper works; cardstock or a photo setting makes the cards last longer.

  2. 02

    Find a calm moment

    Pick a time when your baby is awake, fed and settled, such as after a feed or a nappy change. A few minutes is plenty: little ones work hard just by looking.

  3. 03

    Hold one card close

    Hold a card about 25 to 40 centimetres from your baby’s face, roughly the distance from your chest to your face during a cuddle. An adult always holds the cards.

  4. 04

    Talk softly and pause

    Name the animal in a gentle voice: bear. Then wait. Babies answer with stares, wiggles, coos or wide eyes, and the pause is where the conversation happens.

  5. 05

    Follow your baby’s cues

    When your baby looks away, yawns or wriggles, the session is over. Try a different card another day; the bear will still be there tomorrow.

THE LITTLE BIT OF LEARNING

Why black and white?

A newborn’s vision is still under construction, and contrast is what develops first. Black shapes on a white background are the easiest thing for brand-new eyes to lock onto, which is why high-contrast cards hold a baby’s attention longer than colourful toys. Following a card with their eyes builds early tracking and focus, and hearing you name each animal wires words to what they see. Shared looking is not a lesson: it is your baby’s first conversation.

Make it work for you.

Keep it simple

Newborns to three months love the simplest, boldest shapes. Hold the card still at first, then move it slowly from side to side a few centimetres so your baby can practise following it.

Take it further

From around three months, babies reach and bat. Let them touch the card, tap the bear’s nose and crumple a spare sheet to explore. Around this age, black, white and red pictures become extra interesting.

A note for grown-ups: An adult always holds the cards. Keep paper away from little mouths and out of sleep spaces, and choose a calm moment for card time. Stop when your baby looks away or becomes unsettled: shared looking, not a test.

      FLASHCARD · BLACK AND WHITE BABY CARDS · AGES 0–6 MONTHS

      Bear Flashcard for Babies

      A big, friendly bear face in bold black and white. Newborn eyes lock onto strong outlines first, which is why this card is a favourite first stop. Show it close, say the word softly and let your baby stare for as long as they like.

      Teaching tips

      Say it together

      “Bear! A big, friendly bear.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Hold the card about 30 centimetres from your baby’s face and move it very slowly from side to side. Watching their eyes follow the bear is gentle tracking practice — real work for brand-new eyes.

      Quick parent note

      Your baby may stare hard, blink or go very still. All of that is interest. When they look away, the lesson is over — a good one ends before your baby gets tired.

      FLASHCARD · BLACK AND WHITE BABY CARDS · AGES 0–6 MONTHS

      Bird Flashcard for Babies

      A simple bird with clear wings, drawn in the bold contrast newborns see best. Real birds flap and dart away, but this one is happy to sit still while your baby studies every line.

      Teaching tips

      Say it together

      “Bird. A bird goes flap, flap.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Whisper a little wing sound — flap, flap — and drift the card slowly through the air like a bird landing. Slow is the trick: quick movements are hard for new eyes to follow.

      Quick parent note

      Two to five minutes is a full session at this age. A wide-eyed stare means you have your baby’s whole attention — that is the goal, not a smile.

      FLASHCARD · BLACK AND WHITE BABY CARDS · AGES 0–6 MONTHS

      Butterfly Flashcard for Babies

      A bold butterfly with matching wings, perfect for a baby who is just discovering that two sides can be the same. High-contrast shapes like this hold a newborn’s attention better than any colourful toy.

      Teaching tips

      Say it together

      “Butterfly. Hello, butterfly.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Draw a slow figure eight in the air with the butterfly, about 30 centimetres from your baby’s face. The gentle change of direction gives their eyes something new to follow.

      Quick parent note

      Symmetry is quietly fascinating — grown-ups feel it too. If you catch yourself tracing the wings with a finger while you chat, your baby is watching that as well.

      FLASHCARD · BLACK AND WHITE BABY CARDS · AGES 0–6 MONTHS

      Fish Flashcard for Babies

      A friendly fish with a big round eye and a sweeping tail. The strong black outline is exactly the kind of shape a newborn’s developing vision finds easiest to lock onto.

      Teaching tips

      Say it together

      “Fish. Swim, swim, little fish.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Make the fish swim with a slow, wavy motion in front of your baby, then let the card rest. The rest matters: a still card is when your baby studies the details.

      Quick parent note

      Babies answer in their own way — a stare, a wiggle, a soft coo. Any of those is a conversation. There is nothing to teach and nothing to test here.

      FLASHCARD · BLACK AND WHITE BABY CARDS · AGES 0–6 MONTHS

      Cat Flashcard for Babies

      A black and white cat face with pointed ears and wide eyes. Cats are familiar from storybooks and sofas, which gives you plenty to talk about in your own voice.

      Teaching tips

      Say it together

      “Cat! A cat says meow.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Say meow — softly, because babies startle easily — and see if you get a flicker of attention. Then name the ears, the eyes and the whiskers as you gently point to each one.

      Quick parent note

      Your voice is half the lesson. The same card said warmly, slowly and up close works better than a whole slideshow from far away.

      FLASHCARD · BLACK AND WHITE BABY CARDS · AGES 0–6 MONTHS

      Elephant Flashcard for Babies

      A big elephant with a long trunk, drawn bold for brand-new eyes. It is one of the most striking shapes in the set, and the trunk gives your finger somewhere to go.

      Teaching tips

      Say it together

      “Elephant. Such a big, gentle elephant.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Trace the trunk from top to bottom with your finger, very slowly, while you name it. Then swing your finger gently like a trunk and watch your baby follow.

      Quick parent note

      Big animals invite big, gentle words — huge, slow, soft. Descriptive words like these are lovely early vocabulary, and the elephant makes them fun to say.

      FLASHCARD · BLACK AND WHITE BABY CARDS · AGES 0–6 MONTHS

      Rabbit Flashcard for Babies

      A rabbit with long ears and a round, cheeky face, in the high contrast newborns love. Whiskers, ears and nose give you three easy things to name in one quiet minute.

      Teaching tips

      Say it together

      “Rabbit. Hello, long ears.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Hold two fingers above your head like ears and give them a small hop. Then bring the card close and let your baby study the rabbit’s real ears.

      Quick parent note

      Small silly gestures are not a performance — they are language. Pairing the word rabbit with movement and your happy voice is exactly how first words take root.

      FLASHCARD · BLACK AND WHITE BABY CARDS · AGES 0–6 MONTHS

      Turtle Flashcard for Babies

      A steady turtle in a bold shell. Turtles are wonderfully slow, which makes this the calmest card in the set — a good one for the wind-down part of the day.

      Teaching tips

      Say it together

      “Turtle. Slow and steady, turtle.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Move the turtle the way a turtle would move: barely at all. Then let the card sit perfectly still in your baby’s view and enjoy the quiet together.

      Quick parent note

      Calm card time before a nap can become a lovely ritual. The same three or four cards, the same soft voice — repetition is not boring for babies, it is reassuring.

      FLASHCARD · BLACK AND WHITE BABY CARDS · AGES 0–6 MONTHS

      Ball Flashcard for Babies

      A bold beach ball, round and stripey in black and white. Balls are usually a baby’s first favourite toy, so this card connects straight to play your baby already knows.

      Teaching tips

      Say it together

      “Ball! Round and round, ball.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      From around three months, babies love to bat at things. Hold the card within gentle reach of your baby’s hands and let them tap it — an adult always holds the card.

      Quick parent note

      Reaching is a big deal: it is your baby deciding to join in, not just watch. A swipe that misses is still practice, and there is no wrong way to do this.

      FLASHCARD · BLACK AND WHITE BABY CARDS · AGES 0–6 MONTHS

      Cup Flashcard for Babies

      A simple cup, bold and clear. It is an everyday object your baby will see at every meal, which makes this card an easy bridge between card time and real life.

      Teaching tips

      Say it together

      “Cup. You drink from a cup.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      After card time, show your baby a real cup from a safe distance and say cup again. Same word, two sizes — that jump from picture to world is the whole magic.

      Quick parent note

      You do not need a special moment for this. A card during a nappy change or after a feed is already a complete lesson at this age.

      FLASHCARD · BLACK AND WHITE BABY CARDS · AGES 0–6 MONTHS

      Dog Flashcard for Babies

      A friendly dog face in bold black and white. Dog is a lovely early word because it comes with a sound and an action attached — barking and wagging are easy to act out.

      Teaching tips

      Say it together

      “Dog! A dog says woof.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Say woof in your softest, silliest voice, then pause. If a family dog barks back — the four-legged kind counts — your baby gets the live version too.

      Quick parent note

      Sound effects are not silly extras. Words paired with sounds and your happy face are exactly what early language grows on.

      FLASHCARD · BLACK AND WHITE BABY CARDS · AGES 0–6 MONTHS

      Happy face Flashcard for Babies

      A big bold smiley face. Faces are the very first thing babies love to look at — yours most of all — and this card is a friendly stand-in for when you need both hands free.

      Teaching tips

      Say it together

      “Happy! A happy face.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Show the card, then copy it: make the same big smile and hold it. Babies study faces endlessly, and seeing the card and your smile match up lands beautifully.

      Quick parent note

      If your baby returns even a hint of a smile, treasure it. Either way, the looking is the learning — no performance is required from either of you.

      FLASHCARD · BLACK AND WHITE BABY CARDS · AGES 0–6 MONTHS

      Sleepy face Flashcard for Babies

      A gentle sleepy face with closed eyes. This is the natural last card of a session, and a sweet one to make part of a wind-down or nap ritual.

      Teaching tips

      Say it together

      “Sleepy. Time to rest, sleepy face.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Save this card for last and lower your voice as you show it. Let the room slow down too — dimmer, quieter, slower. Babies read the pace of everything around them.

      Quick parent note

      Pairing a calm card with calm moments builds an association your baby comes to recognise. Do not be surprised if this one becomes the favourite — for you as much as for them.

      FLASHCARD · BLACK AND WHITE BABY CARDS · AGES 0–6 MONTHS

      Spoon Flashcard for Babies

      A bold spoon, plain and familiar. Like the cup, it is an everyday object — and the things a baby sees every single day are exactly the right first words.

      Teaching tips

      Say it together

      “Spoon. Here is the spoon.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Name the spoon on the card, then name the spoon at lunch. Hearing the same word in two places is how a baby learns that words belong to things, everywhere.

      Quick parent note

      Everyday-object cards may feel plain to you, but familiarity is the point. A baby’s first words are overwhelmingly the things they see and hear most often.

      FLASHCARD · BLACK AND WHITE BABY CARDS · AGES 0–6 MONTHS

      Surprised face Flashcard for Babies

      A wide-eyed surprised face, bold and funny. Exaggerated expressions are wonderful for babies, who are busy learning to read faces long before they can read anything else.

      Teaching tips

      Say it together

      “Oh! What a surprised face.”

      Say it naturally, then wait. Whatever comes back — the word, the sound, a point, a giggle — is the right answer.

      Try this

      Make the same face back — eyes wide, mouth round — and hold it a moment, then relax. Face-reading is early people-watching, and babies love it.

      Quick parent note

      Big, slow, clear expressions are easier for a baby to read than subtle ones. This is the one place where overacting is exactly right.
